book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: Open the search box
episodes.subtitle: Why a label cannot explain a search engine

scenes.title: Two questions inside every result
scenes.claim: Admission and ranking are different decisions
scenes.narration: A search box looks small. Behind it is an entire universe of decisions. A paper appears near the top, and we ask: why this one? The preface begins by splitting that mystery in two. Why did the paper enter the candidate set? And why did it rank where it did?

scenes.title: First, who gets to compete?
scenes.claim: The candidate set is the pool available to the next stage
scenes.narration: Imagine a library in space. A gate admits some paper astronauts into a waiting room. That is our illustration of a candidate set. It is a selection, not the entire library. Asking how a paper entered this room is a different question from asking where it stands inside it.

scenes.title: Then, how are candidates ordered?
scenes.claim: A position in the list does not explain admission
scenes.narration: Now the papers in the room are put in order. A record moves upward; another moves downward. This second decision is ranking. Our positions are schematic, not measured scores. A result screen shows the outcome, but it does not automatically reveal the rule that admitted the paper or the rule that ordered it.

scenes.title: Expert searchers meet unfamiliar engines
scenes.claim: The book builds on librarians' existing search expertise
scenes.narration: Aaron Tay describes years of library work in which learning database syntax seemed enough. Around twenty twenty-two, understanding the engine became harder to avoid. His questions were practical: how is this different from Boolean search, how should I enter queries, and which papers will my researchers find?

scenes.title: The words on the box
scenes.claim: Neural • vector • embedding • semantic • agentic • AI-powered
scenes.narration: Meanwhile, the labels multiplied. Neural search. Vector search. Embedding search. Semantic search. Agentic search. A I powered search. These words can point to a representation, a matching method, a pipeline stage, or a marketed capability. Putting them on the same box does not make them interchangeable.

scenes.title: Peel back the label
scenes.claim: No single neural architecture has simply replaced lexical retrieval
scenes.narration: The preface describes a field with several coexisting approaches. No single neural architecture has simply replaced lexical retrieval. A product label leaves the internal choices open. Semantic search, for example, is not another name for dense retrieval. Ask for the mechanism behind the promise, rather than guessing from the promise alone.

scenes.title: What can we actually know?
scenes.claim: Documented facts and unknown internals need different labels
scenes.narration: A better conversation starts with evidence. Which decision happened at which layer? What has the vendor actually documented? What remains unknown outside the company? A librarian does not need to build the engine to ask these questions. But the answer needs more than a slogan on the search box.

scenes.title: Carry two questions with you
scenes.claim: Why admitted? Why ranked here?
scenes.narration: Keep our gate and our ordering platform as two landmarks. Whenever a result surprises you, ask why it was admitted, then why it ranked there. The book develops the machinery needed to keep those questions apart. The next film opens the other mystery: what evidence did an answer never get to see?

episodes.title: The evidence you never see
episodes.subtitle: What citations cannot tell you about retrieval

scenes.title: An answer has two backstage jobs
scenes.claim: Selecting evidence and writing about it can fail differently
scenes.narration: Ask an A I search tool a question. In the preface's picture, one job selects a handful of papers, and another writes about them. Our two machines illustrate those jobs. The final answer joins them together on screen, but selecting evidence and writing about evidence can fail in different ways.

scenes.title: A fluent answer hides its inputs
scenes.claim: The answer does not show the papers it never received
scenes.narration: The writing machine can produce a smooth paragraph with tidy citations. That polish tells us little about the papers available to it. The answer does not show the papers it never received. A missing source leaves no obvious hole in the prose, even when its absence changes the picture.

scenes.title: Check that the reference exists
scenes.claim: Existence checks can expose fabricated citations
scenes.narration: Start with one familiar check: does the cited reference exist? A fabricated citation can fail that test. Our invented paper card is an illustration, not a real citation. Verifying the reference is useful, but passing this first check still leaves two important questions unanswered.

scenes.title: A real paper can be misrepresented
scenes.claim: A real reference does not establish a faithful account
scenes.narration: Does the real paper support what the answer says? A source can exist and still be misrepresented. Picture a valid paper card beside an exaggerated summary. The card's existence does not validate the claim beside it. We must inspect the relationship between the source and the writing.

scenes.title: The quiet failure: missing evidence
scenes.claim: A neat citation list can still rest on an inadequate selection
scenes.narration: Now imagine an important paper stays outside the selection. The answer can remain just as fluent and neatly cited. Yet it is built on a set missing evidence that matters. Our glowing paper is hypothetical; it stands for a source the answer never received. The citation list alone cannot reveal this omission.

scenes.title: Three checks, three different questions
scenes.claim: Existence • faithful writing • adequate retrieval
scenes.narration: Keep three checks separate. Does the reference exist? Does it support the answer's claim? Did retrieval make adequate evidence available? Success at the first does not settle the other two. The preface calls for investigating both writing failures and retrieval failures, because a citation list alone establishes neither faithful writing nor adequate retrieval.

scenes.title: Libraries work with the retrieval half
scenes.claim: Licensing, configuration, comparison, and evaluation need retrieval questions
scenes.narration: Libraries license, configure, evaluate, and pay for search tools. That makes the retrieval half a practical professional concern. Somebody needs enough understanding to compare systems, ask which papers they could reach, and locate a problem in the stack. The aim is useful judgment, without requiring every librarian to become a retrieval engineer.

scenes.title: Follow the evidence before the prose
scenes.claim: The book focuses on how evidence becomes available
scenes.narration: This book concentrates on how evidence becomes available before an answer is written. Answer generation remains outside its main scope. Remember the two backstage jobs, and the paper left outside. The final film explains who the book is for, how it teaches, and which route through it fits your work.

episodes.title: Your route through the book
episodes.subtitle: A field guide for librarians who already know search

scenes.title: Three kinds of search expertise
scenes.claim: Instruction • evidence synthesis • systems and discovery
scenes.narration: The preface meets librarians where they already work. Information literacy librarians teach people to turn questions into searches. Evidence synthesis librarians build and document high recall strategies. Systems and discovery librarians work with configuration, indexes, and integrations. The book begins where these forms of expertise meet the machinery underneath the interface.

scenes.title: Three principles for the climb
scenes.claim: Understanding first • familiar examples • purposeful formulas
scenes.narration: Three principles shape the journey. Understanding comes before detailed mechanism. Examples connect retrieval concepts to familiar library and academic search. Formulas appear where they carry an argument. You need to understand what a scoring method responds to, and what it misses, without calculating every score by hand.

scenes.title: Products move faster than mechanisms
scenes.claim: Named systems are dated illustrations; documentation has limits
scenes.narration: Named products appear as dated illustrations of documented behavior. When the documentation runs out, the book says so. Products will change faster than the underlying mechanisms. A date helps you judge an example's age; it does not turn that example into a current product recommendation. Read the claim and its limits together.

scenes.title: A floor to stand on
scenes.claim: Understand a technical conversation and question a vendor claim
scenes.narration: The destination is a floor to stand on: enough understanding to follow a technical conversation, question a vendor claim, and recognize a retrieval problem. This is not an implementation guide, a product review, or a substitute for a graduate course. It also keeps final answer generation outside its main scope.

scenes.title: Start with the search skills you have
scenes.claim: No prior IR knowledge or mathematical calculation is required
scenes.narration: You can start with little more than Boolean searching. No prior information retrieval knowledge or mathematical calculation is required for the main argument. Reading straight through is the default route. Each part ends with an application exercise: run searches in a tool you can access, and write down what you find.

scenes.title: Choose a shorter route
scenes.claim: Short orientation • instruction • evidence synthesis • procurement • curiosity
scenes.narration: Five shorter routes serve different purposes: a forty-five minute orientation, instruction, evidence synthesis, procurement, and curiosity. The orientation uses summaries and key distinctions. Instruction protects Part One, then follows query transformation, failure, evaluation, and practice. Choose the route for the job in front of you, with links back to the fuller explanations.

scenes.title: Keep the right map open
scenes.claim: Evidence synthesis: Appendix F is core; procurement: keep Appendix D nearby
scenes.narration: For evidence synthesis, focus on Chapter Two, Chapter Eleven, and Chapters Thirteen to Fifteen; Appendix F is core reading on this route. For procurement, use the distinctions, diagnosis, and professional practice chapters, with Appendix D nearby. Already comfortable with Boolean retrieval and B M twenty-five? The curiosity route starts at learnt representations.

scenes.title: Now, to the machine itself
scenes.claim: Ask what happened, at which layer, with what evidence
scenes.narration: You bring the search expertise. The book supplies a map of the machinery. Carry the two opening questions into Chapter One: why did this record get into the candidate set, and why did it rank where it did? Then ask what is documented, what is unknown, and what evidence would help you tell.
